Dermatology · published research

Cosmetic filler-related injection-site reaction

In a 61-person lip-augmentation study, 660-nm red light reduced pain, 808-nm near-infrared light reduced edema, and erythema increased less in treated groups than in controls. Delayed swelling is supported only by case reports, and the broader review is not PBM-specific.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In a 61-person lip-augmentation study, 660-nm red light reduced pain, 808-nm near-infrared light reduced edema, and erythema increased less in treated groups than in controls. Delayed swelling is supported only by case reports, and the broader review is not PBM-specific.

Summary of the Evidence

Four publications form a narrow mapped set: three concern facial filler reactions and one is categorized as a broader injection-site reaction. They include a 61-person non-randomized comparison, two case reports, and a review of six laser studies involving 533 patients. The review includes methods beyond PBM and reuses prior reports, so it is not an additional PBM cohort.

Human and clinical evidence

In the 61-person lip-augmentation study, groups received control care, 660-nm PBM, 808-nm PBM, or both wavelengths. The 660-nm group had greater analgesia, edema decreased only in the 808-nm group, and erythema increased in controls while changing less in PBM groups. The abstract does not clearly describe random allocation or masking (Alvares et al. 2025).

One case used 635-nm red and 830-nm near-infrared LEDs for an injection-site reaction that resolved gradually over seven days (Yoo et al. 2015). Another treated one patient’s delayed swelling years after filler injection with 660- and 808-nm laser exposure. A case cannot show how often the reaction resolves without light (de Melo et al. 2024).

The review reported partial or complete improvement across its six studies, but combined laser methods and indications. Its results cannot be assigned specifically to low-level PBM (Paschoini et al. 2023).

Animal evidence

No animal study was identified in this mapped set.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No cell or ex-vivo study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols used 660-nm red visible and 808-nm near-infrared light, alone or together. The de Melo case reports 2 J per point at 100 mW; Yoo et al. used 635-nm red and 830-nm near-infrared LEDs. The different protocols do not establish a common dose or preferred approach.

Interpretation

In the lip-augmentation comparison, the 660-nm red-light group had greater analgesia, edema decreased only in the 808-nm near-infrared group, and erythema rose in controls but changed less in the PBM groups. The direction therefore differed by symptom and wavelength. Allocation and masking were not clearly described, and delayed swelling is supported by case reports rather than a controlled trial.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term symptoms after lip augmentation Very low for delayed filler-related swelling
Publications and records4 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The 61-person lip-augmentation study reported lower pain with 660-nm red light, reduced edema only with 808-nm near-infrared light, and less erythema increase in treated groups than controls. Allocation and masking were unclear, and delayed swelling is represented by case reports. A masked study with prespecified symptom outcomes and longer follow-up would strengthen confidence.
